images.text:
Kristi: So, I'm beginning to realize how important a great résumé is. It should be worked on carefully and thoughtfully.
Bianca: Of course. A great deal of time must be put into writing a résumé. All of the important facts must be clearly and succinctly spelled out to potential employers.
Kristi: But why do we need a résumé? We could just go in for an interview.
Bianca: The purpose of a résumé is to provide a summary of your skills, abilities and accomplishments. It can show how to fit into your target industry.
Kristi: Yeah, and that's really important because the potential employer wants to know what value you will bring to the company. You need statements that are vivid and that clearly spotlight what you bring to the table over anyone else.

Bianca: I heard that résumés are read over by employers for only seven seconds. They're not reading, they're skimming. So you need to make it clear right off the bat how you can add value.
Kristi: Your résumé is often the first point of contact and it needs to be easy to read. It's expedient if your experience, strengths, and selling points are laid out in brief, bulleted sentences.
Bianca: Did you know that résumés are now looked over by computers?

Kristi: What do you mean?
Bianca: Résumés are fed into a scanner that looks for keywords that the employer is looking for. If the résumé doesn't contain enough of the right keywords, the résumé is thrown out before a person ever looks at it.
Kristi: So how do I know what keywords I need?
Bianca: Maybe you'll find out in the résumé workshop.

Kelly: Hey, Tom. Do you think I need to spend much time on my résumé?
Tom: Yes, it's an important document. It's the first point of contact with a potential employer and it needs to make a good first impression.
Kelly: So what should I put in it?
Tom: It is a summary of your skills, abilities and accomplishments. It shows how you will fit into the job you are applying to.
Kelly: Why do I need to show that?
Tom: The employer needs to know how you can contribute to the company. That needs to be clear right off the bat.

The Simple Present Passive with phrasal verbs

You use an active structure when you want the ‘doer' of the action to be the subject.
You use a passive structure when you want the ‘receiver' of the action to be the subject.
Phrasal verbs are often used in the passive voice.
In active sentences, the thing doing the action is the subject of the sentence and the thing receiving the action is the object. Most sentences are active.

For example:
Active sentence = Employers (subject) read over résumés (object).
In passive sentences, the thing receiving the action is the subject of the sentence and the thing doing the action is optionally included near the end of the sentence.
You can use the passive form if you think that the thing receiving the action is more important or should be emphasized.
You can also use the passive form if you do not know who is doing the action or if you do not want to mention who is doing the action.
[Thing receiving action] + [be] + [past participle of verb] + [by] + [thing doing action]

For example:
Passive sentence = résumés (subject) are read over (by employers).
It is not necessary to mention the object in a passive sentence.
It is common for phrasal verbs to be used in the passive voice. The past participle of the phrasal verb is used and the particle stays the same.

For example:
The résumé is thrown out before a person ever looks at it.

A great résumé is crucial to your job search. There are some elements that must be included in every résumé.
Structure your résumé in an organized manner; keep your font traditional, your layout appealing, and your spacing consistent.
Spell check everything at least twice and have someone else proofread it before you submit it.
List a professional sounding e-mail address and a phone number that is attached to a professional voicemail greeting.

Leave out subjective words like “reliable” and “hard-working.” A potential employer is not going to bring you in for an interview because you say you're reliable. They are going to bring you in because they think you can solve a problem for them.
<span class="strong">5. KEYWORDS FROM THE JOB DESCRIPTION
Incorporate words into your résumé that are listed in the job description of the position you're applying for.

Keep your employment history to the past 10-15 years if you have a substantial amount of industry related experience. If you're a recent graduate, listing the part-time job you had in college is fine.
Make every word you use count and leave lots of white space.
